description: How cost, lifestyle, seasonality, preferences and time shape food choice, and how to cost and modify recipes.
content_html:
Why We Choose the Food We Eat

Walk into any supermarket and you face thousands of choices. The decision you make isn't random — it's shaped by a cluster of interacting factors. Understanding those factors is essential for explaining your own food decisions and for recommending changes to a real person's diet. This lesson maps every factor on the specification and shows how they interact in everyday life.

Physical Activity Level and Energy Needs

Your physical activity level (PAL) directly affects how much energy you need and therefore the foods you choose. A Year 11 student who trains for the school football squad five times a week needs far more carbohydrates and protein than a classmate who is sedentary. A construction worker has a higher PAL than an office worker of the same age, weight and height. High-PAL individuals often gravitate toward energy-dense foods — a building-site packed lunch with hearty sandwiches, savoury snacks and full-sugar drinks — because appetite signals align with genuine energy need.

Key Fact

Total daily energy requirement = BMR × PAL. Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the energy needed at rest; Physical Activity Level (PAL) is the multiplier that accounts for movement. Someone with a high PAL needs more energy and tends to choose larger portions or higher-calorie foods.

Cost and Income

Cost is one of the most powerful drivers of food choice, especially for families on a tight income. A household budget dictates whether a family can afford fresh salmon, ready-prepared stir-fry vegetables or only dried lentils and frozen peas. Food poverty forces people to prioritise filling, low-cost foods — often those high in refined carbohydrates — over nutritionally diverse options. Even for households with moderate incomes, unit prices, special offers and “buy one get one free” promotions directly influence what lands in the trolley. Knowing how to cost a recipe per portion helps you compare the true cost of home cooking against buying ready meals, and often shows that cooking from scratch is cheaper even after factoring in fuel and time.

Preferences, Enjoyment and Habit

People eat food they enjoy. Preference is shaped by familiarity, culture and repeated positive experiences — a child who grows up eating spiced lentil soup will develop different default food preferences to a child raised on plain pasta. Taste preferences also change with age: young children typically prefer sweeter, milder flavours, while adults develop tolerance for bitterness (coffee, dark chocolate). Enjoyment includes texture, aroma and appearance, not just flavour. A meal that smells appealing, looks vibrant and has a varied texture is more likely to be eaten than one that does not, regardless of its nutritional profile.

Healthy Eating and Lifestyle

Awareness of healthy eating guidelines shapes food choice for many people. Someone newly diagnosed with high blood pressure may actively reduce salt and saturated fat, switching to grilled chicken rather than fried and choosing wholegrain bread over white. A university student focused on sport science may track macronutrients carefully. However, lifestyle factors — including shift work, long commutes, caring responsibilities and stress — can override best intentions. A parent working two jobs may rely on ready meals not through ignorance of nutrition, but because time and energy after a 12-hour day are genuinely limited.

Students often assume that people who eat poorly “just don't know better”. In fact, the barrier is usually structural: cost, time, access to fresh produce in their area, cooking facilities or caring responsibilities. A family living in a food desert — an area with no affordable fresh-food retailer nearby — may understand perfectly well that vegetables are nutritious but cannot access or afford them. When you're asked in the exam to explain why someone's diet is poor, look beyond knowledge and consider real-world barriers.

Seasonality and Food Availability

Seasonality affects both price and availability. British strawberries in June are cheap and flavourful; the same strawberries imported from Spain in January cost more and taste blander. Many families adjust menus around seasons: root vegetable stews in autumn and winter, light salads and barbecues in summer. Food availability is also regional — a city with a large South Asian community will have specialist shops stocking fresh curry leaves, paneer and specialist spices that are unavailable in a rural market town. Supply chains, supermarket buying choices and locality all constrain what is realistically available to a shopper.

Time of Day and Time Available

What we eat varies by time of day. Breakfast is typically quick and low-effort — cereal, toast or yoghurt rather than a roast dinner. Evening meals allow more cooking time, so more elaborate recipes become viable. The time available to prepare and cook is a major practical constraint. A 30-minute lunch break permits a simple sandwich or reheated soup; a free Saturday afternoon permits a slow-cooked beef stew. People who work full-time often reserve complex cooking for weekends. Teenagers who arrive home from school at 4 pm and have to be at football training by 6 pm need a meal that can be made in under 30 minutes, which shapes both the ingredients bought and the cooking method used.

Celebration and Occasion

Occasion is a powerful food-choice signal. Christmas, Eid, Diwali and Easter all trigger specific celebratory dishes — roast turkey, biryani, Indian sweets and hot cross buns respectively. Even secular occasions (birthdays, Sunday lunch, a first date) change what people choose. A birthday cake is chosen for its meaning and pleasure, not its nutritional profile. Recognising occasion as a legitimate factor helps students understand why no single meal needs to be “perfectly balanced”: variety over time matters more than a single meal's macronutrient split.

Key Fact

The ten factors influencing food choice are: physical activity level (PAL), food availability, celebration/occasion, cost, preferences, enjoyment, income, healthy eating, lifestyles, seasonality, time of day, and time available to prepare/cook. Every factor can push choices towards or away from a nutritionally balanced diet.

Costing Recipes and Making Modifications

The specification requires you to be able to cost a recipe per portion and to modify a recipe to change its cost, nutritional profile or suitability for a particular eater. Recipe costing involves calculating the price paid per gram (e.g. if 500 g of pasta costs £0.80, then 100 g costs £0.16) and multiplying by the quantity used, then summing all ingredients. Cost per portion = total recipe cost ÷ number of portions. A recipe modification might swap an expensive ingredient for a cheaper one (lamb mince replaced with lentils), reduce waste by using vegetable trimmings in a stock, or increase fibre by adding oats to a crumble topping.

Consider Priya, a 15-year-old swimmer who trains four evenings a week. Her food choices are influenced simultaneously by: her high PAL (she needs more carbohydrates and protein than a sedentary classmate); her family income (her parents shop at a budget supermarket); the time available (she arrives home from training at 8:30 pm, so meals need to be quick); her preference for South Asian flavours (she has grown up eating dhal and rotis); and seasonality (her mum buys British courgettes in summer and tinned tomatoes in winter when fresh are expensive). No single factor dominates — they interact. Understanding this interaction is what top-band exam answers demonstrate.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about food choice, students frequently list factors (“cost, time, preference”) without explaining them. The command word “Explain” means give reasons for and/or causes of — use “because”, “this means that” or “as a result” to link each factor to its effect. For example: “Cost influences food choice because a family on a low income cannot afford fresh fish every week; this means they may rely on cheaper protein sources such as eggs or tinned beans.” Two fully developed points like this will typically earn all 4 marks. Listing four factors with no explanation usually earns only 1 or 2.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food choice is driven by at least ten interacting factors including PAL, cost, income, seasonality, preferences, time available, celebration and healthy-eating awareness — never just one.
  • Food poverty restricts access to a balanced diet through financial and structural barriers, not simply through lack of nutritional knowledge.
  • Recipe costing — calculating cost per portion and modifying recipes — is a practical skill assessed on the written paper; know how to calculate price per gram and cost per portion.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct description of Physical Activity Level (PAL)?
A) The minimum energy needed by the body at rest
B) A multiplier applied to BMR to calculate total daily energy requirement
C) The recommended daily intake of carbohydrates for an active person
D) The percentage of energy that should come from fat
State two factors, other than cost, that could influence a person's food choice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two valid factors from: physical activity level (PAL), food availability, celebration/occasion, preferences, enjoyment, income, healthy eating, lifestyles, seasonality, time of day, time available to prepare/cook. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how seasonality can affect the food choices made by a family when planning their weekly meals.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of what seasonality means (1); description of how it affects availability of specific foods or their price (1); link to how this shapes a family's meal choices, e.g. root vegetable stews in winter, lighter salads in summer (1).

practice_questions.text: Callum is 16 and plays rugby for his school team three times a week. He is planning his weekday meals for the coming term. Explain two reasons why Callum's food choices might be different from those of a classmate who does not play sport.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per reason (2 reasons required). Reason 1: Callum has a higher physical activity level (PAL), which means his total energy requirement is greater; as a result he may choose larger portions or more energy-dense foods such as starchy carbohydrates (1 + 1). Reason 2: his higher muscle-repair needs mean he may prioritise protein-rich foods such as chicken, eggs or dairy, because these supply essential amino acids needed for growth and recovery after training (1 + 1). Other valid explained reasons acceptable (time constraints from training schedule; greater appetite driving larger portion sizes).

practice_questions.text: A recipe for a vegetable curry costs £3.20 in total and serves 4 people. The cook wants to make a modified version that feeds 6 people. She adds an extra 200 g of tinned chickpeas (£0.45 per tin of 400 g) and an extra 150 g of spinach (£0.80 per 200 g bag). Calculate the new cost per portion for the modified recipe serving 6.
practice_questions.marks: Cost of extra chickpeas: 200 g from a 400 g tin at £0.45 = £0.225 (round to £0.23) (1). Cost of extra spinach: 150 g from a 200 g bag at £0.80 = £0.60 (1). New total = £3.20 + £0.23 + £0.60 = £4.03. Cost per portion = £4.03 ÷ 6 = £0.67 (accept £0.67–£0.68). Full credit for correct working shown even if minor rounding differs.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which cost and income are the most important factors influencing the food choices of a family of four living on a limited budget in a British city. In your answer, consider other factors that also affect their choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): sustained evaluation of cost and income as primary drivers (e.g. food poverty restricts access to fresh produce; unit pricing and special offers dominate purchasing decisions; cheap, energy-dense foods chosen over nutritionally diverse options because of affordability). Considers at least two other significant factors (e.g. time available — a working parent with childcare responsibilities has little time to cook from scratch; seasonality — seasonal produce is cheaper and more accessible; lifestyle and habits — preferences formed in childhood persist regardless of income). Reaches a supported judgement: cost and income are highly significant but interact with time and availability; removing financial barriers alone may not change habits without also addressing time and cooking confidence. Uses precise terminology (food poverty, PAL, recipe costing, food availability, seasonality). Applied throughout to a named family context.

Secure (7–9): addresses cost and income with reasonable development; considers at least one other factor with some development; reaches a partial judgement but weighing of evidence is limited.

Developing (4–6): describes cost and possibly one other factor; limited application to the specified family; no clear judgement reached.

Emerging (1–3): simple points about cost or food choice with no development or judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which factor describes the energy a person uses above their resting metabolic rate due to movement and exercise?
A student can't afford fresh salmon and chooses tinned mackerel instead. Which factor most directly explains this choice?
The inability to afford or access a healthy, balanced diet due to financial constraint is known as food _____.
To calculate the cost per portion of a recipe, you divide the total recipe cost by the number of _____ it makes.
Match each factor influencing food choice to its correct description.
right: Events such as birthdays or religious festivals that trigger specific celebratory dishes
The pattern by which foods are naturally available at particular times of year
Daily routines including work hours, caring duties and leisure activities that shape when and what people cook

flashcard_questions.q: What does PAL stand for, and what is it used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical Activity Level; multiplied by BMR to calculate total daily energy requirement.
The inability to afford or access a healthy, balanced diet due to financial constraint.
Calculating the total ingredient cost of a dish and dividing by number of portions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is seasonality in the context of food choice?
flashcard_questions.a: The pattern by which foods are naturally available at specific times of year.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four factors from the spec that influence food choice.
flashcard_questions.a: Cost, time available, seasonality, and physical activity level (PAL).

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a high-PAL individual choose different foods from a sedentary person of the same age?
flashcard_questions.a: They need more energy, so they choose more carbohydrates and larger portions.

flashcard_questions.q: A 500 g bag of pasta costs £0.90. What is the cost per 100 g?
Give one reason why time available affects food choice.
flashcard_questions.a: Limited time means quick or pre-prepared meals are chosen over slow-cooked recipes.

flashcard_questions.q: How does celebration or occasion influence food choice?
flashcard_questions.a: Specific occasions (birthdays, religious festivals) trigger traditional dishes chosen for meaning, not nutrition.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might seasonal produce be preferred on a limited budget?
flashcard_questions.a: Seasonal produce is cheaper and more locally available than out-of-season imports.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula to calculate total daily energy requirement?
Give one structural barrier (not lack of knowledge) that can prevent healthy eating.
flashcard_questions.a: Living in a food desert where affordable fresh produce is not available nearby.

glossary_terms.definition: A multiplier applied to Basal Metabolic Rate to estimate total daily energy requirement, reflecting how active a person is.
The inability to afford or access a healthy, balanced diet due to financial constraint.
The pattern by which certain foods are naturally available at specific times of year, depending on climate, growing conditions and harvest cycles.
Calculating the total ingredient cost of a dish by working out the price per gram or unit of each ingredient and totalling them, then dividing by the number of portions.
